extracted.intended_audience: literate general public, deists/rationalists, critics of Christian scripture, and readers interested in textual/historical criticism of the Bible
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and criteria for judging the authenticity, authorship, chronology, and moral authority of the Bible (with emphasis on internal textual, grammatical, historical, and moral evidence). The work shows how to test testimonial ancient writings and detect later composition, anachronisms, and authors' motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish the Bible's authority before using it as proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Before any thing can be admitted as proved by Bible, the Bible itself must be proved to be true; for if the Bible be not true, or the truth of it be doubtful, it ceases to have authority, and cannot be admitted as proof of any thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept scriptural passages as proof for other claims until you have demonstrated the authenticity and trustworthiness of the Bible itself. Treat appeals to Scripture as circular unless the book's authority is first established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish testimonial books from demonstrative works
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike Euclid's Elements (a book of self-evident demonstration), the books ascribed to Moses, Joshua, Samuel, etc., are books of testimony, and their authority rests upon certainty of authorship and the credit given to their testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply different standards: demonstrative texts (mathematics) stand or fall on internal proof; testimonial texts require independent evidence for authorship and credibility of witnesses. Do not treat testimonial claims as self-evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher evidential standard for extraordinary claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of evidence necessary to establish our belief of things naturally incredible, whether in the Bible or elsewhere, is far greater than that which obtains our belief to natural and probable things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require proportionally stronger proof for miraculous or otherwise incredible assertions (i.e., 'extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence').

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiquity alone is not evidence of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the antiquity of a tale that is an evidence of its truth; on the contrary, it is a symptom of its being fabulous; the origin of every nation is buried in fabulous tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer veracity merely from a story's great age; treat ancient origin as neutral or even suggestive of legendary development rather than proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship inference from internal grammatical/narrative voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The style and manner in which those books are written give no room to believe they were written by Moses; e.g., Exodus, Leviticus and Numbers are in the third person (‘the Lord said unto Moses’), which is the style historians use in speaking of the person whose life they write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use internal linguistic signals (narrative person, voice, framing devices) to test claims of authorship. Third-person narration where first-person would be expected is evidence against claimed authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect composite authorship from dramatic framing and speaker-switching
rubrics_metrics.description: Deuteronomy’s manner is dramatical: a writer opens, introduces Moses 'in the act of speaking,' then resumes, etc.; such framing indicates an anonymous later writer rather than Moses himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify overt framing devices, scene breaks, and interchanges of narrator and speaker as signs of editorial composition or later redaction rather than single original authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal inconsistencies among laws and passages indicate later editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences such as the reason given for keeping the sabbath in Deuteronomy (a memorial of coming out of Egypt) versus Exodus (because God made the heavens and earth in six days) show contradictions and suggest multiple authors or later interpolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare parallel rules/statements across books; significant discrepancies in purpose, wording, or legal content are evidence of composite origin or later alteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anachronisms and chronological markers to date composition
rubrics_metrics.description: References to places or facts that did not exist in the supposed author's time (e.g., pursuing 'unto Dan' when the city was named Laish until centuries later) prove the writing post-dates the claimed period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for place-names, institutions, or referential phrases that must post-date the asserted author; such anachronisms are strong positive evidence of later composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbatim repetition across books indicates dependence and later compilation
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages from Genesis xxxvi appear word for word in 1 Chronicles i; such literal borrowing shows Genesis material was taken from Chronicles and is therefore not older than it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify word-for-word or close-phrase repetitions between books; determine direction of dependence to establish relative dating and whether one work is derivative of another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral coherence test: divine authorship contradicted by immoral commands
rubrics_metrics.description: There are matters in that book, said to be done by the express command of God, that are as shocking to humanity and every idea of moral justice (e.g., wholesale slaughter of men, women, children). To believe the Bible as true one must 'unbelieve all our belief in the moral justice of God.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether alleged divine commands comport with moral reason; pervasive attribution of immoral acts to a deity counts strongly against the claim that the text is inspired by a benevolent omnipotent God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject anonymous testimonial claims for naturally incredible events
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no such thing as forged or invented testimony, neither can there be anonymous testimony, more especially as to things naturally incredible (e.g., talking with God face to face).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand named, reliable witnesses and provenance for testimonial claims of miracles; anonymous or unsigned testimony lacks the weight needed for extraordinary assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for authorial/clerical motive or self-interest in composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer of Deuteronomy was likely a Jewish priest who lived centuries after Moses; priests have been fond of preaching Deuteronomy because it supports tithes—'priests! ye are willing to be compared to an ox, for the sake of tythes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider socio-professional motives (financial, institutional, ideological) that might bias authors toward composing or editing texts to justify privileges or doctrines; such motives weaken claims of disinterested divine revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer internal evidence when disputing scriptural claims with believers
rubrics_metrics.description: Paine confines himself to evidence from the books themselves rather than invoking 'prophane authors' that advocates would contest: 'I will therefore meet them on their own ground, and oppose them with their own weapon, the Bible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing with proponents who accept the text as authoritative, use the text's internal statements and contradictions as the primary basis for critique to avoid irrelevant external authority disputes.
